subtopic: CO-OPERATIVES BRITISH COLUMBIA TEACHERS' INVESTMENT AND HOUSING COOPERATIVE
CO-OPERATIVES BRITISH COLUMBIA TEACHERS' INVESTMENT AND HOUSING COOPERATIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last November the provincially incorporated British Columbia Teachers' Investment and Housing Co-operative went into voluntary receivership. All assets were frozen and the life savings of thousands of active and retired teachers in western Canada were placed in limbo, as the co-op was uniquely structured and deposits were not insured. A restructuring plan has now been approved, according to which members may receive up to 74 per cent of their original deposits. For many this shortfall means a dramatic difference in retirement plans.
Co-op members are asking why Revenue Canada is ignoring the facts and demanding taxes on deposits to which members do not have access. Co-op members are also asking why they can no longer declare capital losses when more affluent Canadians are exempted from taxes on capital gains. Therefore I call upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to bring some fairness into the Income Tax Act. Surely its provisions were never meant to have the effect of depriving retired teachers of their life savings.

subsubtopic: PERCEPTION OF LIFE IN ECONOMIC TERMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of us in this House are against abortion, but we believe in the education of the public on the various means of preventing conception. Proper education solves many problems, especially when that education gives complete understanding of birth control methods and a thorough understanding of the value of human life.
One of the problems for those fighting abortion and the destruction of innocent life is that, while there is proof that life
begins in the initial or very early stages of pregnancy, people are willing to destroy that life to make the social and economic status of the mother more important than the right to life of those who cannot speak for themselves.
To place a utilitarian value on human life and to see each person only in terms of his economic worth can, and will, lead to the destruction of human life and to the murder of those already born who, through mental or physical incapacity, are not able to contribute to society what may be demanded of them by extremists. These and other attempts to negate life, to state that it has no value in itself, must never be tolerated.

subsubtopic: ST. CLAIR RIVER-REAPPEARANCE OF TARRY SUBSTANCE BLOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) promised, with the greatest urgency, to identify the source of the Sarnia blob, which he said was "disfiguring the St. Clair River and causing concern about the quality of the drinking water of thousands of Canadians".
His team of high-powered scientists reported on the situation at the end of January, but failed to identify its source. Meanwhile, new blobs are appearing on the river bottom. It is now the end of June. Divers continue to vacuum up growing amounts of the tarry substance. This month they picked up twice as much material as last month.
Dow does not know where the blob is coming from. Ministry officials do not know where the blob is coming from. Six months have passed and we still do not have the answers. What is going on? What happened to the promised urgency? Why has the Minister not lived up to his commitment to get to the root of this serious environmental problem? If it is more difficult than he thought it was, why does he not level with this House and tell us just what a serious environmental problem we have on our hands there?

subtopic: FUNDING OF CANADIAN FRIENDS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
FUNDING OF CANADIAN FRIENDS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 11 months ago a young man described as a chronic paranoid schizophrenic was ordered by a Scarborough judge to seek hospitalization. When the man went to the hospital he was refused admission on what was later described as a technicality. Some two weeks after the incident he bludgeoned his mother to death with a hammer. I bring this to the attention of the House to drive home how little even our own medical
June 25, 1986

people know about schizophrenia and how important research can be in preventing such gross mishaps.
In Canada we are fortunate to have an organization that addresses this problem, the Canadian Friends of Schizophrenia. This organization, with over 60 chapters across Canada, is devoted to assisting families and promoting general public awareness of this little known and misunderstood disease.
In my view, Friends of Schizophrenia is a classic example of the type of organization that deserves more government funding, and I encourage the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to consider this seriously so that last year's ugly incident remains just that.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CABOT'S LANDING IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 24, 1497, Europeans officially discovered Canada. The leader of the expedition that took possession for England of the entire eastern coast of Canada was Giovanni Caboto, known to us as John Cabot. The entire recorded history of Canada begins from this date.
When we look today at the great contributions the Italian community has made toward Canada's development, it comes as no surprise that the first European to set foot on our land was indeed an Italian. This event adds a perspective of continuity to Canada's multicultural mosaic and points out that Canada's heritage belongs to us all.
We have all benefited from the hard work that Canadians of Italian origin have invested in this land. They have come here like their ancestor, Giovanni Caboto; unlike him, they have stayed to make Canada more prosperous and more versatile. I call on all Canadians to remember and celebrate this important day in Canada's history.

subsubtopic: TESTING OF POISONS AND NERVE GAS

Biological and chemical weapons cannot be used unless troops can be protected against their effects. speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: THE LATE LT. COL. DAVID CURRIE, V.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the death of Lieutenant-Colonel David Vivian Currie, Canada loses one of her authentic heroes. Parliament mourns the loss of a faithful servant of the House where he served valiantly as Sergeant-at-Arms for 17 years.
His sympathy and consideration were experienced over the years by scores of Members of Parliament, both old and new. He had a special place in his heart for new Members, and he went out of his way to initiate them discreetly in the mysterious and sometimes obscure rituals of the House of Commons.
He was an outstanding soldier in the very best sense of the word. Dedication, loyalty, and integrity were his watchwords. Following the war, Colonel Currie moved to Baie Comeau in the pulp and paper business where he remained until 1953, before returning to Montreal. He maintained his interest in military affairs to the end of his life, and was Chairman of the Victoria Cross and George Cross Association headquartered in London, England.
In May, Colonel Currie had an audience with Her Majesty and the Queen Mother at Buckingham Palace. He was accompanied by his wife, Isabel, and 15-year old grandson.
He was of that authentic band of heroes which included Billy Bishop, Barker, and Collishaw in World War I, and Cecil Merritt, Paul Triquet, John Foote, Smokey Smith, Fred Tilston, and John Mahony in World War II. Hon. Members will have noticed that those Canadian names were all holders of the highest award for gallantry-the Victoria Cross. These were in addition to countless others, many of them unhonoured and unsung. His courage and gallantry were of the rare kind which places country above self.
Our hearts go out to his widow and family.
[ Translation]
As a person and in his career, Colonel Currie showed all the qualities of a Canadian dedicated to his country. In wartime and in peace, he understood the vital importance of individual freedom.
To the Parliament of Canada, he added his integrity and dignity as the Sergeant-at-Arms of this House. As a man and as a soldier, he won the respect of his colleagues and fellow citizens. He lived in Baie Comeau for several years after the war and later on in Montreal.
On behalf of the Government and all our colleagues in the House, I wish to extend our sincere condolences to his family.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE LATE LT. COL. DAVID CURRIE, V.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo what the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) has said so well about the passing of Lieutenant-Colonel D. V. Currie, holder of the Victoria Cross. Indeed, Canada has lost an authentic hero.
Those of us who remember him here remember that he was not only a real hero; he looked like a hero. The House of Commons has lost a legendary figure. For 17 or 18 years, Colonel Currie was familiar to the public as the gentleman who carried the Mace and participated on behalf of the House, under the Speaker's guidance, in ceremonial functions of Parliament.
Of course he was much better known to us as Members and to employees of the House as the officer in charge of security, accommodation, furniture, catering-all those details which make this place work.
I suppose those were simpler times, because it always seemed to me that whenever I put a question to him in his capacity as Sergeant-at-Arms, he already had the answer. He never had to look into any file or any book; all those details were at his fingertips. As a stalwart defender of the public purse, his answer to most of the questions we put to him was no.
Under the most vicious enemy fire in war, the Colonel's courage won him the highest military award of what was once the Empire and then the Commonwealth. In peacetime that courage, steadfastness, and aplomb never failed him under the most emphatic demands that this House and Your Honour's predecessors put upon him.

In his dealings with others, Colonel Currie always treated everyone with the utmost respect, from maintenance worker to Prime Minister. He was as available to the average person as he was to the great and the mighty of this country. He was an eminently reasonable and profoundly human man, who under a severe demeanour hid a delightful sense of humour.

He was a devoted servant of this Parliament, putting in long hours, never failing to maintain, in his person and in the office he filled, the dignity and probity of the institution.
June 25, 1986

Canada has indeed lost a great hero. Parliament has lost a loyal servant. Our sympathies go to Mrs. Currie, to his children and to his grandchildren.

subtopic: THE LATE LT. COL. DAVID CURRIE, V.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) in offering the condolences of all members of my Party to the family of Lieutenant-Colonel Currie.
As has already been said, Colonel Currie was among that small band of human beings who demonstrated in the course of their lives truly exceptional courage in fighting not for themselves but for those around them. During the Second World War he led a particular band of Canadians in the course of an action which resulted in the saving of several thousands of Canadian lives in terms of its final consequence. His courage was of that kind of magnitude.
Following that very distinguished service to our country, Lieutenant-Colonel Currie became, as many Members of Parliament will know, a distinguished Sergeant-at-Arms here in the House, a position he always held with great capability and with great distinction. For many of us in the House during the period he was here, we have lost a friend and an acquaintance. Canada has lost a truly distinguished citizen.

The matter of the admissibility of Motions Nos. 1 and 2, in the name of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), is a rather complicated one.
The Chair will recall that the whole issue of whether employees of the House of Commons were subject to the Public Service Staff Relations Act or came under the authority of the Canada Labour Relations Board was challenged in the courts. The Federal Court handed down a ruling that was disappointing for the employees, who nevertheless persevered and took their case to the Supreme Court. On Monday, June 23, the day before yesterday, the Supreme Court received a request to appeal in connection with the matter now before the House.
Since the Supreme Court has not ruled whether the appeal is admissible, and since the motion in the name of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East says specifically that we should, and I will read the motion:
That Bill C-45, be amended in Clause 2 by adding immediately after line 17 at page 1 the following:
"(c) any Supreme Court of Canada decision on certification which shall
take supremacy over this Act."
Since the Supreme Court's decision might be affirmative, that is, favourable to the employees, I think we could argue that the motion is admissible in that it anticipates the possibility that the courts might rule that House of Commons employees are subject to the Canada Labour Code.
That is my only argument, and that is all I wanted to say.
As for Motion No. 2, also in the name of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), this amendment proposes to include the legislation now in effect for federal public servants, that is, the Public Service Employment Act and, of course, the Public Service Staff Relations Act. This is mainly an attempt to include in the Bill the various appeal procedures for appointments and everything that implies.
Here again, there is a good point that can be made, and I did so on second reading, Mr. Speaker, namely that the Public Service Employment Act should apply to House of Commons employees, so that people will know there is a staffing system that is fair and equitable for everyone.
Now I fail to understand why the Chair has grouped 1 and 2, when one motion appeals to the Supreme Court and the other asks for inclusion of an existing Act, an Act of Parliament, an Act concerning staff relations and an Act concerning employment. I do not see why the Chair-perhaps it would care to explain why-I fail to see how one can make a connection between 1 and 2. My point is that No. 2 in particular should be seen as distinct from No. 1, since it has no connection at all with the Supreme Court's decision. In any case, I think the Public Service Employment Act should be included as an amendment to Bill C-45.

speechtext:
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-45, be amended in Clause 4 by striking out lines 11 to 42 at page 6 and lines 1 to 5 at page 7.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is to ensure that this law, which provides collective bargaining and certain other rights to employees of the House of Commons, the Library of Parliament, and the Senate, will also apply to the staff of Members. We are talking about some 1,000 or more employees, since each Member generally has about three employees. The parts which would be diluted according to the amendment are the parts in subclause 4(2) which exclude application of the vast bulk of the Bill to anyone who works for a Member, a Minister of the Crown, a member of the Senate, a Leader, a Whip, or research services connected to any particular caucus.
Throughout debate in committee on Bill C-45, and prior thereto, I did not hear any particularly good reason put forward as to why the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada should in fact exclude totally or almost totally from any kind of employee rights people who work for Members and people who work in the other capacities defined in subclause 4(2). Nor have I heard an explanation of why it is that Members' staff are treated as particularly crucial and yet, for instance, large portions of Ministers' staff are already unionized because they are departmental staff seconded to Ministers' offices. They are doing many of the same jobs which are done by the staff in my office or in the offices of other Hon. Members. Despite the fact that those staff even have the right to strike under certain circumstances, Ministers seem to get by with unionism in their midst in terms of their particular staff.
During the course of the discussion we heard representations based upon the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It was pointed out that very few workers in the entire country were totally excluded from collective bargaining rights. Farm workers and domestic workers in Ontario, or certain categories like those, perhaps hearken back to the days of the domestic servitude. However, in general, working people in every jurisdiction have the acknowledged right to form themselves into unions, to bargain collectively, or to seek to bargain collectively with their employers.
As we have seen in the case of the Gainers strike in Alberta, those rights can be truncated. They can be inadequate, and workers who seek to exercise those rights can be cruelly
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
victimized or very cruelly treated. Nonetheless, in general our Parliaments across Canada have granted those rights.
Employees in positions with the Legislature of Ontario were pointed out as an example. One assumes that those positions are just as crucial as the positions of employees of Members of the House of Commons and the other designated positions excluded in subclause 4(2). Those Ontario employees have the right to form a union and have formed a union. In the case of the employees of the Ontario NDP caucus in the Ontario Legislature, they have in fact had and exercised collective bargaining rights on an amicable basis for some 18 years or 20 years and now have a mature bargaining relationship. Somehow the NDP caucus has been able to continue to move on from one year to the next and has been able to do its job. Occasionally there have been some angry bargaining sessions and some dispute, as there will be between any group of employees and employers. At the same time, difficult situations have very often been resolved in a more equitable and fairer way because of the existence of the union.
For example, after the 1981 provincial election in Ontario, the NDP suffered a set-back and had to cut staff in its bargaining unit. The NDP was able to reach a much more amicable solution to a very difficult situation because it could deal with the staff on a collective basis rather than staff who happened to work for a defeated Member and found themselves out on the street, while other people with perhaps far less seniority and far less experience were able to keep their jobs.
Since Your Honour has ruled other motions out of order, I think 1 can comment generally without straying from the purpose of the motion before us now. When we looked at the question of the status of Members' staff, it was clear that that status was somewhat different from the status of some other employees in the House of Commons. The reason was that Members of Parliament-and I will speak to them, as the largest group-direct, supervise, hire, can fire, and certainly discipline any employees in their offices. The House of Commons pays the cheques, does the administrative work and that kind of thing, but that is all. Therefore, the situation is rather different from that of a supervisor, a foreman or forewoman in a plant or office. They direct, hire, and fire people working for them in a particular section of the plant or in a typing pool or something of that nature. The difference is that in a plant or an office the supervisor, foreman, or forewoman is an employee himself or herself. Members are not employees; they owe their employment to election by their electorate in their individual ridings. They may be accountable within their caucus or under certain rules to you, Mr. Speaker, but basically Members of Parliament are not employees of the House of Commons and are not exercising delegated authority. Even when we admit that, however, it does not stop the fact that as far as the employees are concerned, they tend to be linked not only to the Member but to the caucus to which the Member belongs.

June 25, 1986
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
To a greater or lesser extent the employees of different caucuses work as a unit. For example, training is provided in the three caucuses to employees if there is some caucus priority or campaign on; let us say, the task force on taxation which the current Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) led effectively when his Party was in opposition two years or three years ago. When some priority like that comes into force, Members' staff are pressed into service, working toward some common goals.
It is also the case that the job is stressful and high pressured. People tend to burn out. The present situation is an extremely difficult one for employees if they are given no rights at all. This situation will prevail if the presently proposed form of Bill C-45 goes forward and no change is made. There is still time to make that change.
The only protection provided-and it is an unusual one-is under the unjust dismissal provisions of Part III or Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. That is the only protection being given to Members' staff and to other designated staff in subclause 4(2), the clause which we are discussing right now. Therefore, those employees are supposedly guaranteed a 40-hour week with no more than eight hours of overtime. They are also guaranteed a certain number of holidays and that they will at least be paid the federal minimum wage. They are not paid adequately in most cases for the work they do. Nonetheless, their pay tends to exceed by a significant margin the federal minimum wage, so it is not an issue.
In terms of working hours, there may be certain cases where a Member's employee might decide to seek the protection of the Canada Labour Relations Board, through the Ministry of Labour's inspectors or however, because the individual is being asked to work 50, 55 or 60 hours a week, not just for one or two emergency weeks but on a continuous basis. I think we better be realistic about what that recourse really means for a Member's employee.
Suppose the employee feels that he or she is not being adequately paid for over-time or not being paid at all for overtime, yet is expected to work eight or ten hours extra a week on a continual basis? Suppose that person complains, what happens then? Does someone from the federal Department of Labour or the Canada Labour Relations Board come in to find the Member saying: "You have no right to come in to find out what is happening because this is Parliament and my privileges are being interfered with". That could well occur.
Second, what happens to the employee if an inspector comes in, reads the riot act to the Member, gets the Member to agree that he or she has been working the Member too hard and in future will only work that employee for 40 or 48 hours a week? What happens then, Mr. Speaker? In the first place the Member is free to do it all over again. Second, the Member is also free to take action which will make it extremely difficult for the employee to want to continue. For example, the Member could discipline the employee; suspend the employee
without pay or could demote the employee and give that employee the most menial job of the three or four jobs in the Member's office. The Member could possibly demote the employee in terms of pay as well. While case law would indicate that that amounts to constructive dismissal, and is something that could be debated or disputed in the courts, nonetheless the employee is in a situation where if that employee really wants to fight he or she has to keep on complaining until the Member decides to fire the individual. If an employee is fired, then he or she has the right to go to the Canada Labour Relations Board under the jurisdiction of the unjust dismissal clauses. I am not sure how effective those clauses have been, but it is certainly very flimsy protection for Members staff.
I suggested during the course of the committee hearings that if the Government was not prepared to give collective bargaining rights to employees, at the very least the Government should allow grievances to go to arbitration in the event of discipline, demotion or dismissal. That seems to me to be the very least protection we should give employees who do a vital job on behalf of Members and on behalf of others in other defined areas. I regret very much there was no give at all as far as government Members were concerned on that particular front and that we could take no action there.
I plead with Members opposite in this instance to agree to this amendment which will have the effect, as far as collective bargaining rights are concerned, of bringing into the Bill staff of Members and other staff in the designated areas who are now excluded. The Government pretends it is giving collective bargaining rights to all House of Commons employees but, in fact, the Government is excluding something like one-third of them because of this section, unless it is removed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the amendment which proposes that adjudication expenses be equitably distributed. The way the Bill is now drafted, if there is a dispute with respect to an appointment, a position or a demotion, in other words if an individual learns all of a sudden that he no longer holds his position because he has been demoted, if for one reason or another the individual is the object of an appointment other than the one he holds, Bill C-45 provides that the adjudication expenses are to be shared by the parties involved, namely the employer and the employee.
The amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, as I said, seeks to restore a certain degree of fairness. It is mainly based on the Public Service Employment Act, which now applies to some 275,000 public servants and under which unfair or improper appointments may be appealed.
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
Whenever the Public Service Commission is called upon to appoint an appeal panel, of course the Commission pays the costs; it pays for the services provided in connection with that appeal. Being different, the Labour Code allows employees, through their labour unions, to negotiate matters that are nonnegotiable in the public sector; there is a difference there, and I would like to deal with that, Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal.

We are dealing here with a system that borrows from two pieces of legislation. Under the Canada Labour Code we know that the employees through their unions can negotiate classification standards and procedures. They can also negotiate appointments and promotions, all that affects one's standing in his or her job.
Under the Public Service Employment Act that is not the way it operates. Under the Public Service Employment Act, as I said before, which prevails for approximately 275,000 public servants, the process is different. There is no negotiating of the classification standards between the union and the employer, although the Government promised to bring that in some day. We have not seen any of that yet. You cannot negotiate classification standards and you cannot negotiate nominations or appointments. You cannot make a deal with the employer as to process with regard to such important things as where you stand in the organization, what kind of work you will be doing and what remuneration you will get. It stands as a system by itself distinct from the Canada Labour Code.
Clause 69 of Bill C-45 is the same as Section 97 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act, except for one paragraph which I would like to draw to the attention of the House. Paragraph (4), which was an amendment brought in through committee, says:
Where a grievance respecting a matter referred to in paragraph 63(1 )(d), (e) or (f) is referred to adjudication, the adjudicator's remuneration and expenses shall be borne equally by the parties.
Let us take an example of subsection (f) where an employee finds himself retrograded, that is-

He is being demoted in his own job. The employee could be told by his or her employer, supervisor or office manager; "I am sorry, but you no longer hold the position of a security corporal. You are now holding the position of a junior officer or a simple security guard". The supervisor does not have to provide any reason or any explanation-that is that.
The employee feels hurt and shocked and wants to fight his or her employer's decision, and the only way to do so under Bill C-45 is to ask that the grievance be submitted to arbitration. The arbitrator's expenses and salary will all be payed for by both the employee and the employer. And only when the arbitrator has been appointed is the employee entitled to know

That Bill C-45, be amended in Clause 73 by striking out lines 29 and 30 at page 41.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the section of the Bill put forward by the Government which we thought was the most effective to raise the issue of the denial of the right to strike to people working on Parliament Hill. Clause 73 is a short clause which quite specifically prohibits the right to strike.
During committee stage of the Bill I sought to put forward a number of amendments which essentially would have paralleled the situation that prevails in the Public Service of Canada. It is not a perfect arrangement but it is the provision by which the people in the Public Service have the right to either seek conciliation on the right to strike or, in the event of negotiation breakdown, have their dispute sent to an arbitrator.
There are also provisions within the Public Service which allow for the designation of certain employees as being so essential that they do not enjoy the right to strike. While I regret that those are defined in far too broad a manner, the protection to allow Parliament to continue its work is in that pattern of amendments. For the purposes of this debate, and since the Government has made its position very clear, we have simply asked that Clause 73 of the Bill be deleted. Clause 73 states:
No employee shall participate in a strike.
I presume that means a strike here on Parliament Hill. I suppose they can strike on their part-time job if they must have a part-time job in order to make ends meet.
If the House accepts this amendment, as I hope it will, 1 hope it will also very quickly agree to put in the other necessary pieces of legislation which can be borrowed from the Public Service Staff Relations Act in order to ensure that members of the staff of the House of Commons and Parliament in general will have the same collective bargaining rights as those which exist right now for people working elsewhere in the Public Service of Canada. Obviously, the first step is a step of principle, whether we agree on this issue.
June 25, 1986

We are asked why employees on Parliament Hill should have the right to strike. The answer is, "Why not?". This is a free society. It has always been accepted that in a free society employees should have the right to withdraw their labour in order to arrive at a better version of equality between employers and employees. A strike is a highly orchestrated form of job action. Except in Alberta, employees who strike have their old employment guaranteed for a certain period of time. They do not lose touch completely with their job as they would in an organized workplace if they decided to collectively get together and hand in their resignations. A strike is a way of putting pressure on the employer and dramatizing a situation which has become so crucial that the employees have no other way of getting reasonable consideration of the problem troubling them.
I think Members know that the problem on Parliament Hill is not essentially one of wages or the number of hours per year people are asked to work. It is a matter of job rules, staff classification, and alleged nepotism in appointments to certain positions. If collective bargaining for a couple of years does not start to sort these problems out, then what will happen where employees are tol'd they cannot bargain over classification and staffing because it has been excluded in the Bill? The answer is: I do not know.
Members know that in other jurisdictions, where employees are so incensed at their treatment by employers, the sole effect of a law which says strikes are illegal is that illegal strikes take place. I do not anticipate that that will be the situation here, at least in the near future. Nonetheless, it has been known to occur elsewhere. The Gainers strike in Alberta is perhaps a case in point. If the employees strike for more than 24 hours they effectively lose their jobs. The employer has the right to hire scab workers and is not required to take the employees back and kick the scab workers out when the strike is settled. In the circumstances that is almost a recipe for what is happening out there where the employees feel they have no other recourse.
On Parliament Hill one has to ask whether the people who fix the furniture are essential to the day-to-day operations of Parliament. That is true also of the people who prepare the coffee on the fourth floor of the Wellington Building where almost no Members are located. If there were only two buses running instead of six, would that impede in a material way the work of Parliament for a brief period of time? The record of committee hearings are already several weeks in arrears. If they were to be delayed for a further week or so I would regret it, but if we are not getting them in 24 hours right now and we are still doing our job, then is a strike which delayed them a little longer going to materially affect our ability to do our jobs?
In other words, even on Parliament Hill it should be possible for working people to have the same kind of collective bargaining rights which exist elsewhere. The same kind of disciplines
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
as well. Arbitration is not a particularly good response. Among other things, any arbitrator who comes to resolve a problem here is going to have great difficulty understanding the very unusual environment. It is a very unusual workplace. The people who know best are those who work here all the time, the employees and management.
If a strike is the ultimate recourse, then it very much concentrates the mind when people get down to the nitty-gritty of negotiations. We have seen too many examples in the Public Service of Canada where the employer simply drags his feet, and will not bargain in a meaningful way and in good faith. The attitude is that if they tough it out then it will go to the arbitrator and they will get what they want. They may or may not get what they want, but certainly as far as employees are concerned it is extremely frustrating because they have to leave these issues, on which they are looking for a constructive compromise, in the hands of an arbitrator. On the other side, the employer runs the risk of decisions such as that in Toronto some years ago involving the Metropolitan Toronto Police where it was decided they always had to have two constables in a patrol car. That was something which surely should have been settled by negotiation and not by arbitration.
My time is running short so I hope a few other Members of my caucus will contribute to this debate as well. I do not see why we have to put a glass cage around the Houses of Parliament. We should be an example of progressive, not regressive legislation. Unfortunately, Bill C-45 is the latter. I am quite prepared to admit that it is better than having no Bill at all, but it could have shown quite concretely what the Government meant when it said it wanted to have progressive labour relations across Canada. Clearly that is not the intention of the Government. By denying the right to strike and the other restrictions in this Bill, the Government has created a situation where the employees are getting some bargaining rights but will basically be 20, 30 or 40 years behind where they should be.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to make a few comments because the position of our spokesperson, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, and of our Party generally has been that indeed the last words of the Parliamentary Secretary are the key to the argument, namely that no service has been designated as being essential. Perhaps this is where we would have liked the Government to accept amendments to clear up the situation.
In our view it is neither essential nor necessary to eliminate or take away the right to strike of employees who are not essential to the operations of Parliament. In this respect we also acknowledge the existence of the major academic question of parliamentary privilege: where does it begin and where does it end? We also know full well that this is not an easy question-it is a very complex question-and that many people who are much more intelligent and much more conversant with the matter than we are have been giving serious consideration to it for a number of years.
I remember a citation from Beauchesne's which I looked up and which in my opinion very neatly defines the position of many Members on the right-to-strike provision, and I would like to read it, Mr. Speaker, because I think this puts it very clearly-it is a quote from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms-and it reads as follows:
The control and management of the officers of the Houses are as completely within the privilege of the Houses as any regulation of its own proceedings within its own walls. These officers are under the guidance of certain rules and orders of the House which are among the regulation of its proceedings and as essentially matters of privilege as the appointment of committees, the conduct of public business and the procedure of the Houses, generally, including the acts of the Speaker himself in the Chair. Neither the Government nor any other authority has the power to deal with the staff of the House of Commons unless specially authorized to do so by statute or resolution of the House.
Mr. Speaker, I think Beauchesne comes fairly close to a definition of parliamentary privilege, that employees of the House of Commons are with us in these Parliament buildings and that it is difficult to take a group and say: these people are not essential and those are. This has always been a very difficult matter. We cannot agree entirely with the Government's decision to drop the right to strike from this Bill and decide against giving certain individuals the right to withdraw their services. Considering the wisdom of the people who sat on this committee, I would have thought, and I said so at second reading, that it would be possible to find a definition of what constitutes an essential service: one whose withdrawal jeopardizes either the safety or the well-being of the organization. And that is how it is defined in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. It is also pretty clearly defined in the legislation covering public servants in general, the employees of the Public Service of Canada, which says that a person in a given position is essential and thus excluded from the collective bargaining process and therefore does not have the right to strike, and that others do have the right to strike.
So I would have thought we could have been flexible about this, and I think the employees themselves would also have liked a distinction made between what is essential and what is not. My point is, Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat reluctant to have to admit that with all the assistance we got, we were unable to convince the Government that it was possible to make a distinction between essential and non-essential. We lost on that score, and I must admit that I find this amendment a step backward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was about to say, this is the first time in history that parliamentary employees will be able to enjoy the benefits of contemporary and progressive labour relations legislation which we have tailored to the special circumstances of Parliament. We have given them the ability to enter into collective bargaining. They will also be protected, for the first time ever, under Part III and Part IV of the Canada Labour Code.
I should also like to say that this was my first experience with the legislative committee system. I must say that it is a very satisfactory method by which the House can consider legislation. Our committee operated in the exact way which the McGrath committee planned. There was no partisanship
There was one message which came through loud and clear, and that was a crucial need on the Hill for the provision of a route of redress on staffing matters and on the question of employee classification. The Government brought forward amendments to address those problems. Matters such as the termination of employment of the employee, the demotion of the employee, and the employer's evaluation of an employee's skill, fitness and ability where an employee has been denied an appointment, will now become adjudicable.
These amendments allow for the representatives of both parties, that is the employer and the employee, to select the adjudicator in the case of staffing and classification grievances. In instances where the two parties are unable to agree on the selection of the adjudicator, the amendment would provide for the Chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board to select an independent third party adjudicator to resolve the grievance.
The amendments also provide for independent third party adjudication of classification matters, subject to a provision that there would be a one-year grace period provided in which the administration of the House of Commons, the Library of Parliament, and the Senate will be expected to establish classification standards and procedures and to deal with classification grievances. If the circumstances surrounding the original grievance are still in existence one year after the Bill comes into force, then the employee will have access to adjudication.
Another matter raised in committee was the question of the recognition of cards already signed by employees which must be resubmitted to the Public Service Staff Relations Board. After considering the very reasonable suggestions put forward by the employees, the Government brought forward an amendment which allows the Public Service Staff Relations Board to recognize the union membership cards which were signed by various employee groups on the Hill. This will save the employees a great deal of time in that they will not be forced to obtain new evidence. This will also allow them to embark upon the collective bargaining process that much sooner.

June 25, 1986
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
In fact, Mr. Speaker, if you were to examine the Committee's deliberations and the points put forward by various witnesses, six concerns were raised. Two, namely, third party adjudication on staffing and classification issues and the question of recognizing the union membership cards, were addressed by the Government in committee. Three others, the question of making classification issues and staffing issues negotiable; technological changes and the allowing of union grievances to be presented were considered by the Government. There was a commitment given that if these were to form any part of the forthcoming amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act these amendments would be brought forward simultaneously to the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act.
The last item, the right to strike, was rejected by the Government as it was considered inappropriate to our parliamentary concept.
It is the Government's belief that these amendments go a long way toward giving parliamentary employees a right of redress for staffing and classification issues. It has taken a long time, but parliamentary employees will finally begin to have a say in the determination of their working conditions. We feel this Bill is an important and an historic starting point in this process. I urge the Members to give speedy passage to this Bill at third reading so that our employees on the Hill can begin to enjoy the modern labour management relationship on Parliament Hill which they so richly deserve.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
As I rise on third reading, Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate to emphasize that the debate on Bill C-45 has been both constructive and non-partisan. I suggest it is to the credit of all Hon. Members of the House to stress that it was a substantive debate, and at no time did I hear partisan remarks about this Bill, and I am pleased about that.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-45 is Parliament's response to the need of its employees to form unions to defend their rights as workers. This is not a new issue by any means. I have been in the House for 14 years and practically every year, or every second or third year, the question of a Bill came up. Since the adoption of the Charter in 1982-as Hon. Members are aware, it acknowledges the right of Canadians to form associations-this question has become more urgent and the employees of the House of Commons saw fit to take action.
When we consider the Government's decision to introduce Bill C-45, a piece of legislation that is both complex and important, "An Act respecting employment and employer and employee relations in the Senate, the House of Commons and the Library of Parliament", I think the subject of this legislation and the way it was dealt with is first of all, to the credit of the employees themselves, who, as we know, promoted the concept of organizing and obtained the support of their colleagues at work. Mr. Speaker, today it is recognized that
the cards signed by the employees before the Bill was tabled had the effect of advancing and promoting the concept of union organizing on Parliament Hill.
Mr. Speaker, it is also a fact that these cards and this initiative were the result of work done by people at all levels, people who were concerned about employee-employer relations and about instances of unfairness to employees which were sometimes impossible to remedy.
We were unable to include the right to strike in the Bill, Mr. Speaker, and as I said earlier when we were considering the amendments, I would have preferred to see employees designated or identified according to whether they were essential or non-essential to parliamentary operations. I quoted Beauchesne because, whether we like it or not, parliamentary privilege prevails, and I am convinced that all employees are part of the parliamentary unit and as such, we are all dependent on and bound to one another by the concept of parliamentary privilege. The majority won. Perhaps one day, we might be able to do something else.
The major provisions of the Bill, as the Parliamentary Secretary said a while ago, deal mostly with the right of appeal to a third party about matters as serious as dismissal, demotion, refusal of a promotion or misapplication of norms of classification. We must clearly understand, Mr. Speaker, that, in Bill C-45, the Government is not agreeing to the negotiation of norms of classification, because there will be no negotiation about what people will do, only about application of the norms to determine whether the work done by the employee corresponds with the classification level, which will naturally have been determined by the employer.
There is a difference and I hope that it is clear. The norms of classification will not be negotiable; what will be negotiable will be their application. Staffing will be negotiable, but I imagine that the job description will be determined by the employer and it is how the position will be filled that will be negotiable, which I believe to be a good thing. In any case, it was because of these two problems, staffing and classification, that the employees worked persistently for many years to obtain the right to unionize so that there would be some fairness in the system, so that their rights as employees would be guaranteed, and so that, if they deem it appropriate, they would be able to obtain redress in case of an injustice or an unfair treatment.
Mr. Speaker, amendments to certain terms in the French text were put forward in committee, as well as a number of minor technical amendments which I shall not be dealing with.
But I would like to return to the matter I consider important, important enough to warrant an amendment-arbitration to resolve grievances.
It is quite clear to me that all that was sought was a requirement for the employer to pay for the expenses incurred with respect to appeals or grievances that might be lodged by employees. The Government has deemed fit not to support that amendment, and it will be saying in Bill C-45 that the
June 25, 1986

expenses relating to grievances shall be borne by both employer and employee. The people in charge, that is the third parties, incur expenses of course, and this will be borne by both the employer and the employee. In other terms, where there is a conflict or grievance concerning a staffing decision, promotion or demotion, dismissal or lay-off, such matters will henceforth be referred to a third party, but the employee shall bear half of the expenses, his share of the expenses incurred by the arbitrator, the conciliator or the person who will be in charge of resolving the grievance.
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House believe that such a practice is not what we are accustomed to. At the federal level we operate differently with our 250,000-odd federal civil servants. What we have there is an appeal procedure that is identical to the grievance procedure put forward in C-45, except that under the appeal procedure, which is administered by the Public Service Commission of Canada, expenses are entirely paid for by the general public, the public Treasury through the Commission. This means that employees can appeal without having to spend money.
This is why we introduced the amendment. It was turned down, which admittedly is a defeat, but the idea was good. It was worthwhile in my view.
I do not want to speak too long on this Bill but I would like to state clearly that I believe Bill C-45 provides the House of Commons, the Senate, and the Library of Parliament with a framework of representation which is, I hope, in the interests of all employees. Issues of concern included provision in the Bill for grievance procedure, job classification, staffing, appointments, appraisals, promotions, demotions, transfers and lay-offs which could not be subject to an arbitral award. The exclusion of political staff and the denial to employees of the right to strike has been addressed by everyone in the House, and the conclusions are quite evident.
During committee hearings a number of amendments were proposed by the Government which have, at least in part, met the concerns of employees. The stronger grievance procedure which I just described will come into force after one year. This can be dealt with positively and will be a step in the right direction. With the introduction and acceptance of some amendments the legislation is better. It improves the process with regard to justice and equity. Bill C-45 does not allow for the transfer of certification orders without a vote of the members of the union. NABET believes that this will add to the delay for the union.
I would like to put some of the concerns of the Public Service Alliance on the record. PSAC believes that the grievance procedure is an improvement but does not go far enough. It will act as a basis for future negotiations but does not meet with PSAC approval. PSAC would like the union to be able to take policy issues to grievance. This is not allowed under the amended legislation. PSAC is concerned about the
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
one year the employer has been granted to reorganize classifications. Until the one year is up, the unions cannot grieve anything regarding classification.
In conclusion, I would like to say that my colleague, the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), has participated in debate on this issue, was in committee, and did her utmost to improve this Bill. Speaking in her name and the name of my colleagues I would like to join with all other parliamentarians in hoping that Bill C-45, an Act respecting unionization on the Hill, will meet the hopes and expectations of our employees. Anything can be improved, as I am sure this Bill can be.
I believe we are today taking a historic step in the right direction. I know that the employees are anxious to operate effectively under this legislation. I know there will be some wrinkles to be ironed out. We have taken a non-partisan approach on this Bill. Canadians have a commitment to giving employees' organizations the right to get the best deal possible with the employer. I join all of my colleagues in telling the employees that we are happy and proud that they pushed us into doing this. We are very happy and proud that they have succeeded in getting something which they have wanted to obtain for a long time. We wish them the best.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all pleased that the process on Bill C-45 is coming to an end because it has been long and time consuming. I am not sure what position the Liberal Party is taking on third reading of the Bill, but although we have acted this afternoon to expedite the Bill in order to ensure that it will receive approval by the Senate before the end of this week, we will oppose the Bill at third reading because my Party feels that, although it is a step forward to have some form of labour relations legislation for employees on Parliament Hill 120 years or so after Confederation, it is bad to have a Bill as flawed as this one. We regret that some fundamental changes have not been made in the Bill in order to recognize that Members' staffs should have the same bargaining rights as employees in the private sector and elsewhere in the Government of Canada.
When this process began we were told that the aim was to give employees on Parliament Hill the same bargaining rights which they would enjoy if they worked for the Public Service of Canada. There is a bit of a con game being played because what is provided in Bill C-45 is considerably less than that. One reason is that the Public Service of Canada has a long history of labour relations behind it now. There is a very intricate and elaborate network of consultation on many subjects which cannot be bargained under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. There is the Public Service Commission, nominally responsible to Parliament, which is in place to ensure that the merit principle is respected. There is a well-established process under which employees who feel they have been badly treated in staffing actions can appeal to the PSC. There is a similar process by which classification decisions can be subject to a review outside of an employee's particular department, although still granted by management. What that

June 25, 1986
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
means is that the negotiated portion of what goes on in the Public Service of Canada is part of a complex of labour relations mechanisms and institutions, and simply to take a stripped down version of the negotiation part and say that the employees on the Hill are getting it all is to seriously mislead those who look to see what is happening.
The Government erred fundamentally in not understanding that, because of the independence of Parliament from the Government of Canada, it was not possible to put the House of Commons under the Public Service Staff Relations Act or something close to it. It was not possible to give the PSC direct oversight on actions taken by the administration of the House of Commons on behalf of MPs and senators. Therefore, it seems more creativity was needed in coming up with an acceptable Bill to give our employees what they do not have. Of course, I do not comment on the fact that the Government has quite specifically refused to grant the right to strike even though it has been available to people in the Public Service for 20 years.
I would remind the House that in 1966 the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons, which was then studying Bill C-170, which ultimately became the Public Service Staff Relations Act, stated that consideration should be given to introduction of legislation to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act and the Library of Parliament Act to extend to the employees the advantages and rights similar to those of public servants under Bill C-170. It is now 18 years later and we are just about to conclude debate on Bill C-45, yet we still have not gone as far as what was proposed by that committee then. I think it was understood at that time that there would be early action, but unfortunately it has been deferred. One has to blame the Liberal Government because it could have done this but did not. For all its faults one has to recognize, and I do, that the Conservatives have gone forward with a Bill which gives a form of bargaining, not to all but to many employees on Parliament Hill. Even if it has defects, it will at least ensure that employees will be able to talk over issues, be consulted and make representations to the administration, something they have not been able to do before.
That said, I would point out that while certain changes were made during the committee process, a process which was relatively positive, nonetheless, when it came to looking at solutions to problems, the Government cracked the whip and undue restrictions were put on a number of amendments which we were able to make to the Bill, even though those that were made were welcome. One unchanged area was the scope of arbitration. As people who have studied these matters are aware, that effectively governs the scope of bargaining. If you do not have the right to strike and only have recourse to arbitration to resolve disputes, then those matters which go to arbitration are the only ones on which you can have meaningful negotiations. The other matters will not be capable of adequate negotiation because the employer will say that there is no requirement on him to discuss them. They can simply be
allowed to sit on the table without response and the union will not be abled to get any satisfaction through arbitration because the arbitrator will note be able to touch it. For example, Clause 55(2) says:
No arbitral award shall deal with the standards, procedures or processes governing the appointment, appraisal, promotion, demotion, transfer, lay-off or release of employees, or with any term or condition of employment of employees that was not a subject of negotiation between the parties during the period before arbitration was requested in respect thereof.
Clause 55(3) says:
An arbitral award shall deal only with terms and conditions of employment of employees in the bargaining unit in respect of which the request for arbitration was made.
In other words, very little can be bargained. As well, Clause 5 limits that even further. That clause is a management's rights clause which is much stronger than you find in the private sector. Clause 5(3) says:
Nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to affect the right or authority of an employer to determine the organization of the employer and to assign duties and classify positions of employment.
In other words, there is no way employees can directly get at many of the problems which provoked them into all the effort which has preceded the introduction of this Bill.
This Bill is technically not an expansion of rights, it is a diminution of rights. For a period of six months the Canada Labour Relations Board had certified some 1,000 employees on Parliament Hill. Those employees therefore enjoyed the full collective bargaining rights available under the Canada Labour Relations Code which is as ample a code as exists in Canada. That has now been taken away. On the pretext that the Government's rules for its employees shall be followed, the Government has gone forward with a set of rules which take away the certifications granted by the Board. That fails to recognize the efforts the unions put into getting that certification. The Government then applies a number of other restrictions.
It should be clear that there were other reasons for which the workers formed unions than that of wages and benefits. They were concerned because their dignity as workers was being threatened. They were concerned because they felt there were a lot of injustices in things such as classification and staffing. They were concerned that there was no meaningful grievance process on Parliament Hill. Grievances could be lodged but the final stage was with management and there was no outside arbitration. When that is the case, of course, a grievance process can never work particularly effectively. They were concerned about arbitrary management action. They were concerned about what they felt was evidence of nepotism in various places. They were concerned about documented instances of sexual harassment. They were concerned about the fact that there were substantially different salaries being paid to workers who were doing essentially the same job. They were concerned that health and safety was not being respected for employees on Parliament Hill. They were concerned that, almost alone among employees under federal jurisdiction, or what they thought was federal jurisdiction, they did not have
June 25, 1986

the fundamental right to form a union, freely associate, bargain collectively, and enforce collective bargaining by recourse to a strike.
What has come down the pipe? Bill C-45. It does not grant the right to strike. It restricts collective bargaining. It totally excludes Members' staff, apart from the question of their being able to seek adjudication on unjust dismissal. If they do so, they will have no union representative at their side in order to help them fight that particular case. They will either have to get grace and favour assistance from the union, which is doing it because it believes that the Members' staff should be represented, or they will have to hire a lawyer at great expense in order to fight that particular case.
I am sure you know that the staff of the Members of the House of Commons are not that well paid, and for many of them that will be a further hardship and sacrifice if they have to use legal counsel in order to take a case before an outside arbitrator in the event of unjust dismissal. If they complain in public, they will be liable to dismissal.
I was disappointed that the Liberals, when we came to the vote just a few minutes ago on my amendment, which would have extended collective bargaining rights to Members' staff, were no more progressive on this issue than the Progressive Conservatives. They agreed with the Government's stand that next to no rights should be given to Members' staff.
What progress was there during the course of the committee hearings? Well, three things occurred. We broadened the title of the Bill to include the Library of Parliament. I think that was my contribution as the Librarian of Parliament is a constituent and I was simply acting on behalf of an elector in my riding.
The Government brought forward amendments, which were accepted, to extend grievance rights to allow grievances to go to arbitration respecting discipline, demotion and dismissal, and respecting the questions of classification and staffing. The Parliamentary Secretary in committee indicated publicly-and I have just checked this with him and confirmed it-that although the Government has not been prepared to agree to the negotiation of issues of staffing or classification for parliamentary staff, the Government is prepared to use its good offices, through the Board of Internal Economy, to ensure that the administration of the House of Commons will consult with the staff through the unions which have been formed on issues of classification and staffing. I will be watching, as one Member who, among other things, has many of the affected employees in my riding, to ensure that that particular commitment is respected.
During the hearings, there was real concern, which I think was felt by Members on all sides, including my friend for Nepean-Carleton, the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) and the Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), Conservative Members who took part in the hearings, and I think we all
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
felt real misgivings about the quality of the labour relations administration at the House of Commons. It was symbolized by the fact that the House was extremely reluctant to agree to any participation on paid time by the presidents of the three unions, who got certification so they could see what was going on and as well help Members in the work. At the same time, the House saw nothing at all wrong with having as many as 15 or 20 management staff from the House of Commons sit in on many of our hearings. That kind of inequity spoke to us about an attitude within the House of Commons which helps to account for the fact that the workers have unionized. They have been very unhappy about what has been going on, and the House of Commons does not yet appear to have learned very much.
I have already commented on whether or not the rights that have been granted are the same as those that Public Service workers have. I would comment on the fact that the concession with respect to certification is a very minor one. These three unions were already recognized. It would have been perfectly easy for the Bill to have extended the CLRB recognition to those three unions, the Alliance, NABET and the security staff, without the people having to go and get certification again.
In passing I want to say a very sincere thank you for the very constructive and helpful participation from the Alliance, from the Parliament Hill local of the Alliance, and also to Mr. Jacques Audette and Allan Piche, who were particularly helpful to me, and to all of the other people from the other unions who took part, gave us information and were extremely helpful. I am afraid that their help was not repaid in this particular area because the concession on certification is a very minor one. For reasons of certainty I have been advising the unions that it may make sense for them to get new cards, because they can get automatic certification, we were told, if they get 51 per cent of their bargaining unit with new cards.
I regret the fact that, given the peculiar circumstances in the House of Commons, the Government was not prepared to grant policy grievances to the unions on Parliament Hill. This is a different place from the Public Service. In the Public Service there is a network of consultation mechanisms, which I mentioned before, which has taken 40 years to build up. We have not got the time to do all of that catching up. Allowing what are called policy grievances or union grievances to be taken collectively would have anticipated problems and helped to sort things out much more quickly, and I think would have been an appropriate way of dealing with some of the special conditions that are here, particularly since most workers across the country have it.
I welcome-even if I am dismayed at the delay-the assurance from the Parliamentary Secretary that the issues of technological change and negotiation of staffing will be incorporated in this Bill if they become part of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. I believe they should have been included now, but it is better to have them later than not to have them at all. I have already stated my disagreement with

June 25, 1986
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
the Government in terms of its antediluvian view on the question of the right to strike.
I have two final comments to make on this particular Bill, which, as I said before, we are opposing. We are opposing it on principle because it still is inadequate labour legislation. What has been done during the course of the hearings-and everyone did contribute positively to them-is to turn a Bill, which was totally unacceptable to the workers involved, into a Bill which they perforce feel they have no choice but to accept. It is the only game in town. Nonetheless, the amendments put forward by the Government that allow grievances through arbitration by individuals on matters of classification and staffing and that kind of thing are the barest minimum to make the Bill barely tolerable to the unions. While we do not have to go along with that, I understand the desire to get the Bill through.
I feel very strongly personally about the total exclusion of Members' staff from this Bill. I think that is wrong and I think we are going to discover it is wrong when sometime in the next year or two we get some staff members from different Members' offices-hopefully not the New Democratic Party- who feel compelled to go to the public and make a public issue of some complaint or some problem because they have no redress and no recourse, having been left out of Bill C-45.
I feel particularly strongly over the fundamental denial of collective bargaining rights because of the denial of the right to strike. I feel that the limitations on bargaining are such that it makes this a very bad Bill. I would say in conclusion that good labour relations are very important. I hope that the Speaker, the acting Administrator of the House of Commons, and the Board of Internal Economy members who are not listening will see these comments in Hansard.
The House of Commons is back in the dark ages in terms of its labour relations. It must take Bill C-45, inadequate as it may be, seriously. It must seek harmony in labour relations, accepting fully that workers who have chosen to form trade unions are exercising a right available to all Canadians, and not a begrudging kind of attitude that has gone on until now when the House is trying to take those rights away.
If that were to be the spirit in which Bill C-45 is administered by the House of Commons, then it has some prospects of working. If the current attitude persists, it has no opportunity to work at all. I hope it will work for the sake of the employees affected. I am sorry the Bill could not have been a better one.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on this Bill and recall that this is a historic piece of legislation.
In fact, Parliament is at last responding to the wishes of its employees to organize for the purpose of defending their rights.
I remember, in the last months of the last Parliament, that a parliamentary committee consisting of representatives of all three political groups, had been trying to reach agreement on a Bill that would get unanimous consent before the last election, a Bill that would have given our employees on the Hill the right to organize a union and defend their interests in a more direct and orderly fashion from then on.
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognizes the right of any group of workers to organize in order to defend themselves against any abuse of authority by the employer, and since we in Parliament adopt legislation to set certain standards for Canadian companies in their relations with their employees, the fact that Parliament had yet to give its employees the right to organize was becoming an altogether embarrassing and anachronistic situation.
I think the Government's Bill is a step in the right direction. Of course, it does not go as far as I personally would have liked, but I must admit the Government has made some progress. I understand that I am to continue my speech after Private Members' Business, at seven o'clock.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-208 whose purpose is to change the name of Ottawa Airport to National Capital Airport, for we can say that the airport serves the region of the capital of Canada which is located in the Province of Ontario and the Province of Quebec.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government might clear up an anomaly which now exists in the air transport sector in the National Capital Region. As I said a moment ago, this anomaly is that the airport is located in the National Capital Region and this is why the purpose if this Bill is to change the name to National Capital International Airport.
If we go back in history, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want to prolong the debate on this question, we have to remember that symbols should be displayed so that Canada's capital may become the National Capital Region of Canada, not located only in Ottawa which, for all practical purposes, is an Ontario city. Local residents must identify with the national capital of Canada, and this kind of symbol is the only way to make it into a real capital for all Canadians. It has to be the soul of the Canadian nation. Canadians must develop this kind of nationalist spirit which is so sorely lacking. For all practical purposes we are a new country, hardly a few hundred years old.
For merely 20 years or so, we have had a flag which is a national symbol and a source of pride for many Canadians, but I suggest we should do something to enhance this pride by making our national capital the true heart and soul of the Canadian nation.

Only in this way can certain disparities between the two sectors be overcome-

-and real freedom of choice of residence made meaningful in the capital area.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in the debate on Bill C-208 which is sponsored by my colleague from the riding of Hull-Aylmer and whose purpose is to change the name Ottawa International Airport to Ottawa-Hull International Airport.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill cannot be considered as being very important since it involves a minor name change for the airport which serves us all in the national capital. But still it is a name change which is rather symbolic, and we ought to know that symbols are really important, and perhaps they have more significance when they have to do with the very nature of our country. This is why I support the Bill of my colleague from Hull-Aylmer.
We recently had an example of what can happen when the symbolism goes wrong in terms of the relationship between the two major municipalities in the national capital. Regardless of the growing size of Gatineau or of the importance of the cities of Nepean and Gloucester in terms of population, it is still the case that the two major municipalities in the National Capital Region are the cities of Ottawa and Hull.
One very refreshing and encouraging development of the last six years while Marion Dewar was Mayor of Ottawa was the rapprochement between the City of Ottawa and the City of Hull. There were meetings between municipal councillors Mayor Dewar was on very good personal terms with Michel Legere, who has now been the Mayor of Hull for three years
June 25, 1986

or four years. They communicated on upcoming issues and sought to come up with a common position.
One fine symbolic example of the friendshp which exists between the City of Ottawa and its sister city on the other side of the river was that on Canada Day the Mayor of Ottawa led a group of citizens and councillors across the Interprovincial Bridge where they met in the middle with the Mayor of Hull and a group of his councillors and citizens.
Just a few weeks ago the Canada's Capital Visitors and Convention Bureau voted that in future the tourist publicity for Ottawa-Hull, which has used the proposed name for the airport in the Bill of my hon. colleague, should in fact only use the name of Ottawa. It said that in marketing terms this might make some sense. The move was supported by the new Mayor of Ottawa, Mr. James Durrell.
I am afraid that single gesture did terrible damage in terms of harming the constructive and mature relationship which has developed between Ottawa and Hull and between Ottawa area municipalities and those of the Outaouais. It is clear that personal relationships between the two mayors have been deteriorating, I suspect largely because of actions by the Mayor of Ottawa. Shortly thereafter the Mayor of Ottawa announced that rather than take the citizens of this community across the river to meet with their counterparts in Hull on Canada Day, he would have brunch with senior citizens at Lansdowne Park. No one objects to him having brunch with senior citizens; it is a good thing to do. However, there is no reason that he could not have brunch with them at ten o'clock and then meet with the Mayor of Hull and the citizens of Hull at twelve o'clock or something like that. Once again it looked like and it was a slap in the face, not only to the Mayor of Hull but to all citizens on the Quebec side.
We have a community in the National Capital Region which is heavily bilingual. If we look at the proportions of the population in the National Capital Region on both sides of the Ottawa River, we are just about a microcosm of the country. Some 25 per cent are French-speaking in the National Capital Region. Obviously it is a higher proportion in Hull than it is in Ottawa. Nonetheless, this city more than any other city in Canada, with perhaps the exception of Moncton, is a city in which one grows accustomed to the fact that one hears French and English side by side, wholly accepted and used commonly by people on the buses, people in the stores, people in offices and everywhere else.
In marketing terms it might be difficult for people to think of Ottawa-Hull rather than only Ottawa. Yet, the reason for doing it is that this is an awkward country and we should somehow make it survive. We are French and we are English. We are stretched right across 4,000 miles. We should have a name which reflects in tourist literature the bicultural identity which we have here.
The Mayor of Ottawa said that Hull does not reflect the ethnic composition of the people who live on that side. Well, Ottawa does not do so either. If it did, we would all be native
Ottawa International Airport
peoples; we would be from Canada's first peoples, not from second or third generations by way of immigration in the last 200 years or 300 years.
In supporting this particular Bill, I think it is a symbolic way of indicating the nature of the national capital. If one wanted to find a name upon which people could agree, we could use as an example the name of the airport at Toronto. It might be a good idea too. However, if we are to call it by the name of the city or cities served, I suggest that the House of Commons should in fact take the lead, particularly after the slights by a politician at another level of government who does not seem to understand the symbolic importance of ensuring that our duality-our dual cultures and our dual languages-is reflected in all things we do in the nation's capital. Of course, this is not just in Ottawa nor just in the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. The nation's capital includes as large an area on the Hull side as it does in Ottawa, and certainly Hull is very much an integral part of the national capital. Thanks to developments of the last few years, it has a substantial proportion of the public servants who work in the national capital.
